Data preprocessing of gut microbiota cohorts

Author

Mariam Rahali Masbouri

Published

March 22, 2026

In this first section, the relevant datasets are imported from the dysbiotic cohorts (that is, those pertaining to IBD, IBS, CRC, and CDI) as well as the healthy cohorts from the Human Microbiome Project (HMPv13 and HMPv35), NIBIOHN and MORINAGA cohorts, and a “diet intervention” cohort as well. The datasets are available at these following links:

  • For dysbiotic cohorts (in 01-dysbiotic-cohorts.qmd):

    • IBD cohort: https://ibdmdb.org/results
    • IBS cohort: https://data.mendeley.com/datasets/29n2z5r5ph/3
    • CRC cohort: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-019-0458-7
    • CDI cohort: https://github.com/grp-bork/cdifficile_Ferretti_2022/tree/main/data/CDI

  • For healthy cohorts (in 02-healthy-cohorts.qmd):

    • HMPv13 and HMPv35: https://github.com/twbattaglia/MicrobeDS/tree/master/data
    • NIBIOHN and MORINAGA cohorts: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12866-021-02215-0
    • Diet intervention cohort: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36079725/

Supplementary cohorts will also be used in the analyses, and they will be imported in the third section (see 03-supplementary-cohorts.qmd):

  • IBD cohort without time series (Fransoza et al. 2019): https://www.nature.com/articles/s41564-018-0306-4
  • IBD cohort with time series (Halfvarson et al., 2017): https://www.nature.com/articles/nmicrobiol20174

The final output will be a MAE (MultiAssayExperiment) object, containing data that has been cleaned and rarefied for the downstream analyses.

Dysbiotic cohorts

In this section, we will first import the relevant datasets from the dysbiotic cohorts (that is, those pertaining to IBD, IBS, CRC, and CDI), and then perform several descriptive analyses for each of those datasets. The analyses will include: data cleaning, taxonomic aggregation (if necessary) and rarefaction.

We will transform each dataset into a phyloseq object, before merging them into a MultiAssayExperiment object in the last section. For this we need:

  • abundance data, a matrix of relative abundance with samples as rows and features (taxa) as columns.
  • taxonomy data, a data frame with features (taxa) as rows and taxonomic levels as columns.
  • samples data, a data frame with samples as rows and metadata variables as columns.

TODO: Create dictionaries for metadata variables for each dataset, to keep track of the meaning of each variable and the values they can take, previous and new name, and if it is kept for further analysis or not.

IBD dataset (Lloyd-Price et al. 2019)

The inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) dataset was obtained from the IBDMDB, with the results published in Lloyd-Price et al. (2019). The authors of the Science paper did not provide information to which study name the IBD dataset comes from, so the HMP2 study was chosen, which seems like a reasonable choice since it is the most recent study on this page.

Stool samples were initially collected from 132 participants at multiple time points. Specifically, samples were collected at baseline (that is after the initial colonoscopy, which was used to stratify participants into healthy controls, Crohn’s disease (CD) patients, and ulcerative colitis (UC) patients), and then every 2 weeks for 1 years.

Metagenomics (MGX) were performed on 1638 stool samples; DNA was quantified, normalized, and used to prepare sequencing libraries with the Nextera XT kit. Libraries were pooled, quality-checked, and sequenced on an Illumina HiSeq platform to generate ~10 million paired-end reads per sample. Raw sequencing data was then demultiplexed and converted to standard file formats (BAM and FASTQ files) using the Picard suite.

For the analyses, we have the following datasets at our disposal:

  • hmp2_metadata.csv: contains the metadata for the samples.

From Metagenomics (MGX) and products sections, we have the following file available:

  • taxonomic_profiles.biom.gz: contains the taxonomic profiles and relative abundance data for stool samples, in BIOM format.

In the chunks below, we import the metadata and taxonomic profile for the IBD dataset.

Code 
# Importing the metadata

metadata <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir(), "01-raw-data/01-IBD", "hmp2_metadata_2018-08-20.csv"), col_types = cols(.default = "c"))

# Importing the taxonomic profiles

data <- read_biom(file.path(data_dir(), "01-raw-data/01-IBD", "taxonomic_profiles.biom"))

For abundance data, we need to filter the taxonomic profiles to keep only the bacterial species relevant for our analyses, and to remove the taxonomic levels from the taxonomic names by keeping only the last available level.

Code 
df <- data |> biom_data() |> as.matrix() |> t() |> as.data.frame() 
abundance <- df |> select(contains("k__Bacteria"))

names(abundance) <- str_extract(names(abundance), "[^|]+$")

df |> pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "feature", values_to = "rel_ab") |> 
  filter(rel_ab == 1, feature != "k__Bacteria") |>
  gt(caption = "Features with relative abundance of 1")

For taxonomy data, we need to extract the taxonomic levels and names from the taxonomic profiles, and to keep only the last available level for each feature, saved as taxon_names, with a letter indicating the taxonomic level between parentheses (e.g., “g” for genus, “f” for family, etc.). Additionally, we also filter the dataset to only keep the “Bacteria” kingdom, since we are only interested in bacterial taxa for our analyses.

Code 
taxonomy <- 
  tibble(full_name = names(df)) |>
  mutate(
    kingdom = str_extract(full_name, "k__[^|]+"),
    phylum = str_extract(full_name, "p__[^|]+"),
    class = str_extract(full_name, "c__[^|]+"),
    order = str_extract(full_name, "o__[^|]+"),
    family = str_extract(full_name, "f__[^|]+"),
    genus = str_extract(full_name, "g__[^|]+"),
    species = str_extract(full_name, "s__[^|]+")
  ) |>
  mutate(
    taxon = coalesce(
      species, genus, family, order, class, phylum, kingdom
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    taxon_name = coalesce(
      str_remove(species, "s__"),
      str_c(str_remove(genus, "g__"), " (g)"),
      str_c(str_remove(family, "f__"), " (f)"),
      str_c(str_remove(order, "o__"), " (o)"),
      str_c(str_remove(class, "c__"), " (c)"),
      str_c(str_remove(phylum, "p__"), " (p)"),
      str_c(str_remove(kingdom, "k__"), " (k)")
    )
  ) |>
  filter(kingdom == "k__Bacteria") |>
  select(-full_name)
Note

In the supplementary code provided, the authors filtered out taxa with _unclassified annotation. Also, they are also _nonname taxa, but they did not filter those out. I filter out both _unclassified and _noname taxa, but I am not sure if this is the right choice. Should we filter out both _unclassified and _noname taxa, or only _unclassified taxa?

We document below how many features have _unclassified or _noname annotation at each taxonomic level.

Code 
taxonomy |>
  summarise(across(c(kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species), list(
    unclassified = ~ sum(str_detect(., "_unclassified"), na.rm = TRUE),
    noname = ~ sum(str_detect(., "_noname"), na.rm = TRUE)
  ))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(),
               names_to = c("level", "type"),
               names_sep = "_(?=unclassified|noname)",
               values_to = "n") |>
  mutate(level = factor(level, levels = c("kingdom", "phylum", "class", "order", "family", "genus", "species"))) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = type, y = fct_rev(level), fill = n) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_label(aes(label = n), size = 4) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "dodgerblue") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Count",
       subtitle = "Unclassified / noname annotations per taxonomic level")

For taxa samples, several taxa have the same taxonomic annotation, so we need to aggregate the abundance data by taxonomic annotation, and to keep only one row for each taxon in the taxonomy data.

The duplicates are documented below, with the taxonomic annotation and the number of features with this annotation.

Code 
taxonomy |> group_by(taxon_name) |> summarise(n = n()) |> filter(n > 1) |>
  gt(caption = "Taxonomic annotation with duplicates") |>
  tab_options(
    container.height = px(400)
  )

Since abundance data is in relative scale, we can simply sum the relative abundance of features with the same taxonomic annotation to get the relative abundance of the taxon.

Code 
abundance <-
  abundance |>
  t() |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  bind_cols(taxonomy |> select(taxon)) |>
  group_by(taxon) |>
  summarise(across(everything(), sum)) |>
  column_to_rownames("taxon") |>
  t() |>
  as.data.frame()

abundance |> head() |> select(1:5)

CSM5MCUO                 0         0.0009106                      0  0.0000488

CSM5MCW6                 0         0.0000958                      0  0.0000000

         c__Bacteroidetes_noname

We also need to filter the taxonomy data to keep only one row for each taxon, and to set the taxon names as row names.

Code 
taxonomy <- 
  taxonomy |> 
  distinct(taxon, .keep_all = TRUE) |> 
  column_to_rownames("taxon")

taxonomy |> glimpse()
Rows: 809
Columns: 8
$ kingdom    <chr> "k__Bacteria", "k__Bacteria", "k__Bacteria", "k__Bacteria",…
$ phylum     <chr> NA, "p__Acidobacteria", "p__Acidobacteria", "p__Acidobacter…
$ class      <chr> NA, NA, "c__Acidobacteriia", "c__Acidobacteriia", "c__Acido…
$ order      <chr> NA, NA, NA, "o__Acidobacteriales", "o__Acidobacteriales", "…
$ family     <chr> NA, NA, NA, NA, "f__Acidobacteriaceae", "f__Acidobacteriace…
$ genus      <chr> NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, "g__Granulicella", "g__Granulicella", "…
$ species    <chr> NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, "s__Granulicella_unclassified", NA,…
$ taxon_name <chr> "Bacteria (k)", "Acidobacteria (p)", "Acidobacteriia (c)", …

Since the IBD dataset contains higher level taxonomic annotations in addition to species level annotations, we can also create a phyloseq object with only species level annotations, by filtering the taxonomy data to keep only species level annotations, and modify the abundance data accordingly.

Additionally, we also filter out species for which _unclassified or _noname annotation is present.

Code 
taxonomy <- 
  taxonomy |> 
  rownames_to_column("taxon") |>
  filter(!is.na(species)) |> 
  column_to_rownames("taxon") |>
  filter(!str_detect(species, "_unclassified|_noname"))
Code 
abundance <- 
  abundance |>
  t() |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("taxon") |>
  filter(taxon %in% rownames(taxonomy)) |> 
  column_to_rownames("taxon") |>
  mutate(across(everything(), as.numeric)) |>
  t() |>
  as.data.frame()

We check if samples rows sum to 1.

Code 
row_sums <- rowSums(abundance)

if (all(row_sums == 1)) {
  cat("All samples rows sum to 1.\n")
} else {
  cat("Not all samples rows sum to 1.\n")
}
Not all samples rows sum to 1.
Code 
row_sums |> summary()
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  0.000   1.802   1.888   1.832   1.941   2.000

We renormalize the abundance data to make sure that all samples rows sum to 1 and discard samples for which the sum of relative abundance is 0 (i.e., samples for which we do not have any bacterial species annotation after filtering out unclassified and noname species).

Code 
dropped <- rownames(abundance)[rowSums(abundance) == 0]
cat("Dropped samples:\n"); print(dropped)
Dropped samples:
[1] "CSM7KOOR"    "MSM6J2HB"    "PSM6XBSU_TR" "PSM6XBTD"    "PSM7J129"   
[6] "PSM7J1AW"    "PSM7J1BH"    "PSMA266C"
Code 
abundance <- abundance[rowSums(abundance) != 0, ] |> (\(x) x / rowSums(x))()

rowSums(abundance) |> summary()
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
      1       1       1       1       1       1

We check if there are any singletons (i.e., taxa that are present in only one sample) in the dataset, and if so, we document them by showing the taxonomic annotation and the number of samples with this annotation.

Code 
abundance |> 
  rownames_to_column("sample_id") |>
  pivot_longer(-sample_id, names_to = "taxon", values_to = "rel_ab") |>
  filter(rel_ab > 0.05) |>
  group_by(taxon) |>
  mutate(singleton = ifelse(n() == 1, "Singleton", "Non-singleton")) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(singleton == "Singleton") |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = taxon, y = sample_id, fill = rel_ab) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "blue", labels = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(x = "Taxon", y = "Sample ID", fill = "Relative abundance",
       subtitle = "Singleton taxa where rel_ab > 5% (present in only one sample)") +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )
Note

The singletons in the dataset should not pose a problem for the downstream analyses, since they have a low relative abundance.

We also document the distribution of the number of taxa per sample, as well as the mean relative abundance across samples over all taxa.

Code 
abundance |> 
  rownames_to_column("sample_id") |>
  pivot_longer(-sample_id, names_to = "taxon", values_to = "rel_ab") |>
  filter(rel_ab > 0) |>
  group_by(sample_id) |>
  summarise(n_taxa = n()) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = n_taxa) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  labs(x = "Number of taxa", y = "Number of samples",
       subtitle = "Distribution of the number of taxa per sample") +

abundance |> 
  rownames_to_column("sample_id") |>
  pivot_longer(-sample_id, names_to = "taxon", values_to = "rel_ab") |>
  filter(rel_ab > 0) |>
  group_by(sample_id) |>
  summarise(mean_rel_ab = mean(rel_ab)) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = mean_rel_ab) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  labs(x = "Mean relative abundance", y = "Number of samples",
       subtitle = "Distribution of the mean relative abundance across samples") +

  plot_layout(nrow = 2)
Code 
abundance |>
  rownames_to_column("sample_id") |>
  pivot_longer(-sample_id, names_to = "taxon", values_to = "rel_ab") |>
  filter(rel_ab == 1) |>
  gt(caption = "Samples with a taxon with relative abundance of 1")
Samples with a taxon with relative abundance of 1
sample_id taxon rel_ab
HSM7J4LH s__Faecalibacterium_prausnitzii 1
Warning

A sample has a taxon with relative abundance of 1. This means that this sample has only one taxon with non-zero relative abundance. However, this taxon was not identified above (before the renormalization), so this is likely due the renormalization step.

For samples data, we need to filter the metadata to keep only the samples for which we have metagenomics data, and to set the sample IDs as row names. Additionally, since not all covariates in the metadata are relevant for our analyses, we also select only a subset of the metadata variables to keep in the samples data.

We document (some) of the original metadata variables in the plots below.

Code 
# we filter out columns with only NA values

metadata_filtered <- metadata |> filter(data_type == "metagenomics") |> select(where(~!all(is.na(.x))))
samples <- metadata |> clean_names() |> filter(data_type == "metagenomics") |> select(where(~!all(is.na(.x))))
Code 
samples |>
  filter(!is.na(age_at_diagnosis)) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = diagnosis, y = age_at_diagnosis |> as.numeric(), fill = diagnosis, color = diagnosis) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.4, color = NA) + 
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.2), size = 1, alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("nonIBD" = "#0078B9", "CD" = "#EA0017", "UC" = "#FF7F0E")) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("nonIBD" = "#0078B9", "CD" = "#EA0017", "UC" = "#FF7F0E")) +
  labs(x = "", y = "Age", fill = "Diagnosis", color = "Diagnosis",
       subtitle = "Distribution of age across diagnosis groups") +
  
  samples |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = education_level, fill = diagnosis) +
  geom_bar(position = "stack") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("nonIBD" = "#0078B9", "CD" = "#EA0017", "UC" = "#FF7F0E")) +
  labs(y = "", x = "Education level", fill = "Diagnosis",
       subtitle = "Distribution of education level \nacross diagnosis groups") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1)) +
  
  samples |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = occupation, fill = diagnosis) +
  geom_bar(position = "stack") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("nonIBD" = "#0078B9", "CD" = "#EA0017", "UC" = "#FF7F0E")) +
  labs(y = "", x = "Occupation", fill = "Diagnosis",
       subtitle = "Distribution of occupation across diagnosis groups") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1)) +
  
  samples |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = diagnosis, fill = diagnosis) +
  geom_bar(position = "stack") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("nonIBD" = "#0078B9", "CD" = "#EA0017", "UC" = "#FF7F0E")) +
  labs(y = "", x = "", fill = "Diagnosis",
       subtitle = "Distribution of diagnosis groups") +
  
  plot_layout(nrow = 2)
Note

There is no age data for the healthy group, since healthy participants were not diagnosed with IBD, so they do not have an age at diagnosis.

The selected variables are: “Project”, “External ID”, “Participant ID”, “data_type”, “week_num”, “visit_num”, “IntervalName”, and “diagnosis”.

Code 
samples <- 
  metadata |> 
  select("External ID", "Participant ID", "data_type", "week_num", "visit_num", "IntervalName", "diagnosis") |>
  clean_names() |>
  filter(data_type == "metagenomics") |>
  column_to_rownames("external_id")

We also filter out the dropped samples (for which the sum of relative abundance is 0) from the samples data.

Code 
samples <- 
  samples |> 
  rownames_to_column("sample_id") |>
  filter(!sample_id %in% dropped) |>
  column_to_rownames("sample_id")
Code 
samples |>
  rownames_to_column("sample_id") |>
  select(sample_id, participant_id, visit_num, week_num, interval_name, diagnosis) |>
  group_by(visit_num, participant_id) |>
  mutate(total_samples = n()) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = participant_id, fill = diagnosis) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Participant ID", y = "Number of samples", fill = "Diagnosis",
       subtitle = "Number of samples per participant and diagnosis") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1))

Finally, we can create the phyloseq object using the otu_table, tax_table, and sample_data functions from the phyloseq package.

Code 
ps_ibd <- phyloseq(
  otu_table(as.matrix(abundance), taxa_are_rows = FALSE),
  tax_table(as.matrix(taxonomy)),
  sample_data(samples)
)

ps_ibd
phyloseq-class experiment-level object
otu_table()   OTU Table:         [ 432 taxa and 1630 samples ]
sample_data() Sample Data:       [ 1630 samples by 6 sample variables ]
tax_table()   Taxonomy Table:    [ 432 taxa by 8 taxonomic ranks ]

IBS dataset (Mars et al., 2020)

The irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) dataset in Mars et al. (2020) was obtained from Mendeley data plateform.

Metagenomics were performed for 474 stool samples recolted from 77 participants, separated into healthy controls (H), constipation predominant (IBS-C), diarrhea predominant (IBS-D), or mixed (IBS-M). DNA was extracted from stool samples using the QIAGEN PowerSoil kit and quantified by NanoDrop and PicoGreen assays. Shotgun metagenomic libraries were prepared using a modified Nextera XT protocol and sequenced on either a HiSeq 2500 or NextSeq platform with single-end reads. Samples from three cohorts were randomly distributed across two sequencing runs to reduce batch effects. Reads were trimmed to 100 bp and aligned to a prokaryotic reference genome collection at 97% identity using BURST, with low-depth samples (< 10,000 reads) removed. Functional profiles were generated using KEGG Orthology annotations, and low-abundance gene estimates were further improved using SHOGUN.

For the analyses, we have the following datasets at our disposal:

  • metagenomics.xlsx: contains the metagenomics count data and metadata for biopsy samples, in CSV format. This correspond to the file “Supplementary data I Microbiome data tables stool and biopsy.xlsx” in the plateform (version 3 from 2020-03-11).

In the chunk below, we import the metadata and abundance data for the IBS dataset.

Code 
data_biopsy <- readxl::read_excel(file.path(data_dir(), "01-raw-data/02-IBS", "metagenomics.xlsx"), sheet = 2)
metadata <- readxl::read_excel(file.path(data_dir(), "01-raw-data/02-IBS", "metagenomics.xlsx"), sheet = 5)

We will transform the abundance data into a phyloseq object in the next steps, but before that, we need to perform some data cleaning. For this, we need to filter the abundance data to keep only bacterial species, and to remove the taxonomic levels from the taxonomic names by keeping only the last available level.

Code 
abundance <- data_biopsy |> filter(str_detect(`#OTU ID`, "k__Bacteria"))

For taxonomy data, we need to extract the taxonomic levels and names from the taxonomic profiles (OTU column in data_biopsy), and to keep only the last available level for each feature, saved as taxon_names, with a letter indicating the taxonomic level between parentheses (e.g., “g” for genus, “f” for family, etc.).

Code 
taxonomy <-
  tibble(full_name = abundance$`#OTU ID`) |>
  mutate(
    kingdom = str_extract(full_name, "k__[^;]+"),
    phylum = str_extract(full_name, "p__[^;]+"),
    class = str_extract(full_name, "c__[^;]+"),
    order = str_extract(full_name, "o__[^;]+"),
    family = str_extract(full_name, "f__[^;]+"),
    genus = str_extract(full_name, "g__[^;]+"),
    species = str_extract(full_name, "s__[^;]+")
  ) |>
    mutate(
    taxon = coalesce(
      species, genus, family, order, class, phylum, kingdom
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    across(c(species, genus, family, order, class, phylum, kingdom), 
           ~ str_remove_all(., "\\[|\\]")),
    taxon_name = coalesce(
      str_remove(species, "s__"),
      str_c(str_remove(genus, "g__"), " (g)"),
      str_c(str_remove(family, "f__"), " (f)"),
      str_c(str_remove(order, "o__"), " (o)"),
      str_c(str_remove(class, "c__"), " (c)"),
      str_c(str_remove(phylum, "p__"), " (p)"),
      str_c(str_remove(kingdom, "k__"), " (k)")
    )
  ) |>
  select(-full_name)

We check if there are any missing species annotations.

Code

To merge duplicates in abundance, we can simply sum the counts of features with the same taxonomic annotation to get the count of the taxon.

Code 
abundance <-
  abundance |>
  bind_cols(taxonomy |> select(taxon)) |>
  group_by(taxon) |>
  summarise(across(-`#OTU ID`, sum)) |>
  column_to_rownames("taxon")

We check if there are any singletons (i.e., taxa that are present in only one sample) in the dataset, and if so, we document them by showing the taxonomic annotation and the number of samples with this annotation.

Code 
abundance |> 
  rownames_to_column("taxon") |>
  pivot_longer(-taxon, names_to = "sample_id", values_to = "counts") |>
  group_by(sample_id) |>
  mutate(rel_ab = counts / sum(counts)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(-counts) |>
  filter(rel_ab > 0.05) |>
  group_by(taxon) |>
  mutate(singleton = ifelse(n() == 1, "Singleton", "Non-singleton")) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(singleton == "Singleton") |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = taxon, y = sample_id, fill = rel_ab) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "blue", labels = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(x = "Taxon", y = "Sample ID", fill = "Relative abundance",
       subtitle = "Singleton taxa where rel_ab > 5% (present in only one sample)") +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )

We also document the distribution of the number of taxa per sample, as well as the mean counts across samples over all taxa.

Code 
abundance |> 
  rownames_to_column("sample_id") |>
  pivot_longer(-sample_id, names_to = "taxon", values_to = "count") |>
  group_by(sample_id) |>
  mutate(rel_ab = count / sum(count)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(rel_ab > 0) |>
  group_by(sample_id) |>
  summarise(n_taxa = n()) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = n_taxa) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  labs(x = "Number of taxa", y = "Number of samples",
       subtitle = "Distribution of the number of taxa per sample") +

abundance |> 
  rownames_to_column("sample_id") |>
  pivot_longer(-sample_id, names_to = "taxon", values_to = "count") |>
  group_by(sample_id) |>
  summarise(mean_count = mean(count)) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = mean_count |> log10()) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  labs(x = "Mean counts", y = "Number of samples",
       subtitle = "Distribution of the mean counts across samples") +

  plot_layout(nrow = 2)

We will then rarefy the IBS dataset, so that all samples have the same sequencing depth, and filter out low-abundance taxa. We will use the rrarefy function from the vegan package to perform rarefaction.

First, we separate the dataset into two groups: “healthy” and “diseased” so that rarefaction (and prevalence filtering) is performed separately for the two groups, to avoid biasing the results by removing more samples from one group than the other.

Code 
tmp <-
  abundance |>
  rownames_to_column("taxon") |>
  pivot_longer(-taxon, names_to = "sample_id", values_to = "count") |>
  left_join(
    samples |> rownames_to_column("sample_id") |> select(sample_id, cohort)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    status = ifelse(cohort == "H", "Healthy", "Diseased")
  )
Code 
tmp_healthy <- tmp |> filter(status == "Healthy")
tmp_diseased <- tmp |> filter(status == "Diseased")

We show the distribution of sequencing depth across samples, to choose a rarefaction depth.

Note

Note that a classical rarefaction threshold would be to simply take the median depth, but in this case, we choose to take the median depth divided by 2, to keep more samples in the dataset, especially given the relatively small number of samples in the IBS dataset.

Code 
tmp_healthy |>
  group_by(sample_id) |>
  summarise(depth = sum(count)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = depth)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = median(depth)/2), color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Sequencing depth", y = "Number of samples", caption = "Red dashed line represent median depth divided by 2",
       subtitle = "Distribution of sequencing depth across healthy samples")
Code 
tmp_diseased |>
  group_by(sample_id) |>
  summarise(depth = sum(count)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = depth)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = median(depth)/2), color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Sequencing depth", y = "Number of samples", caption = "Red dashed line represent median depth divided by 2",
       subtitle = "Distribution of sequencing depth across diseased samples")

CRC dataset (Yachida et al., 2019)

The colorectal cancer (CRC) dataset in Yashida et al. (2019) was obtained from the DDBJ Sequence Read Archive (DRA) under the names DRA006684 and DRA008156; however, those are raw sequencing data, and the authors mentioned having used only processed datasets.

Processed datasets seems to be available as Supplementary Tables, therefore these will be used for the subsequent analyses.

Stool samples were collected after bowel prep and stored on dry ice. DNA was extracted using bead-beating with a GNOME kit, quality-checked by TapeStation, and stored at −80°C. Sequencing libraries were prepared with the Nextera XT kit and verified for quality before paired-end whole-genome shotgun sequencing on an Illumina HiSeq 2500, generating 150 bp reads with a target output of 5 Gb per sample.

The samples were classified into nine groups according to colonoscopic and histological findings:

  • normal (no remarkable colonoscopic findings) and a few polyps (up to two small (<5 mm) polyps) were classified as “Healthy”;
  • multiple polypoid adenomas with low-grade dysplasia and polypoid adenoma(s) with high-grade dysplasia were classified as “MP”;
  • stage 0 CRC was classified as “Stage_0”;
  • stage I CRC and stage II CRC were classified as “Stage_I_II”;
  • stage III CRC and stage IV CRC were classified as “Stage_III_IV”.
  • the remaining group was normal with a history of colorectal surgery, and was classified as “HS”.

We have the following datasets at our disposal:

  • 41591_2019_458_MOESM3_ESM.xlsx: contains the processed datasets for stool samples, in Excel format. This correspond to the file “Supplementary data 3.xlsx” in the article (version 1 from 2019-11-28).

We import those datasets in the chunks below.

Code 
data <- read_xlsx(file.path(data_dir(), "01-raw-data/03-CRC", "41591_2019_458_MOESM3_ESM.xlsx"), skip = 3, sheet = 13)

metadata <- read_xlsx(file.path(data_dir(), "01-raw-data/03-CRC", "41591_2019_458_MOESM3_ESM.xlsx"), skip = 2, sheet = 4)

As in the previous datasets, we need to perform some data cleaning before creating the phyloseq object. For abundance data, we need to filter the dataset to keep only bacterial species.

First, we notice that the number of samples in metadata and abundance data do not match, so we need to filter the abundance data to keep only samples for which we have metadata.

Code 
abundance <- data |> select(any_of(metadata$Subject_ID))

Now, we see that we have 616samples in metadata, and 615 samples in abundance data, so there is still a mismatch between the two datasets. We document this below.

Code 
setdiff(metadata$Subject_ID, colnames(abundance))
[1] "00001"

After checking manually, we see that this sample is present in the metadata, but not in the abundance data, so we can simply filter it out from the metadata.

Code 
metadata <- metadata |> filter(!Subject_ID %in% setdiff(metadata$Subject_ID, colnames(abundance)))

We create the taxonomy data in the next few steps.

Note

We see here that we do not have the complete taxonomy lineage for the features in the abundance data, but only the last available taxonomic level (e.g., species). This will make it difficult to filter the dataset to keep only bacterial species, since we do not have the taxonomic annotation for the kingdom level. Can we assume that all species are bacteria and go ahead with the analyses?

We first create the taxonomy table by extracting the taxonomic annotation from the feature names in the abundance data, and by keeping only the last available level for each feature, saved as taxon_names.

Code 
taxonomy <- 
  tibble(full_name =  data[1] |> pull()) |>
  filter(!str_detect(full_name, "-1")) |>
  mutate(
    taxon_name = full_name,
    kingdom = "k_Bacteria",
    phylum = NA,
    class = NA,
    order = NA,
    family = NA,
    genus = str_c("g_", word(taxon_name, 1)),
    species = case_when(
      word(taxon_name, 2) == "sp." ~ NA,
      is.na(word(taxon_name, 2)) ~ NA,
      TRUE ~ str_c("s_", word(taxon_name, 2)),
    ),
    taxon = taxon_name
  ) |>
  select(kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species, taxon_name, taxon)

We check if there are duplicates in taxa species, and document them below.

Code 
taxonomy |> 
  group_by(taxon_name) |> 
  summarise(n = n()) |> 
  filter(n > 1) |>
  gt(caption = "Taxonomic annotation with duplicates")
Taxonomic annotation with duplicates
taxon_name n

No duplicates are found in the taxonomic annotation, so we can keep all features in the abundance data, and we can simply set the taxonomic annotation as row names for the taxonomy data.

CDI dataset (Ferretti et al., 2023)

The Clostridium difficile infection (CDI) metagenomics dataset was obtained from the Github repository associated with the original article from Ferretti et al. (2023). [indicate the date of the latest version for these datasets].

For the analysis, we have the following datasets at our disposal:

  • CDI_mergedControl_samples.csv: contains metadata for both control and CDI samples, in CSV format.
  • mOTU20_profiles_filteredCDI.csv: contains abundance count data for stool samples, in CSV format.
  • motus_taxonomy.csv: contains the taxonomic annotation for the features in the abundance data, in CSV format.

In the chunks below, we will import the metadata, abundance data, and taxonomic annotation for the CDI dataset.

Code 
metadata <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir(), "01-raw-data/04-CDI", "CDI_mergedControl_samples.csv"))
abundance <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir(), "01-raw-data/04-CDI", "mOTU20_profiles_filteredCDI.csv"))
taxonomy <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir(), "01-raw-data/04-CDI", "motus_taxonomy.csv"))
Note

Interestingly, this dataset contains samples from different study (and thus different sequencing protocols).

Note

We see here that we do not have the complete taxonomy lineage for the features in the abundance data, but only the last available taxonomic level (e.g., species). This will make it difficult to filter the dataset to keep only bacterial species, since we do not have the taxonomic annotation for the kingdom level. Can we assume that all species are bacteria and go ahead with the analyses?

First, we need to filter taxonomy data to merge taxon with the same taxonomic annotation, and to keep only one row for each taxon, with the taxonomic annotation as row names. Additionally, we fill the taxonomic levels based on the taxonomic annotation.

Code 
taxonomy <- 
  taxonomy |>
  mutate(
    taxon_name = coalesce(
      str_remove(mOTU_name, "\\[.*\\]")),
    kingdom = "k_Bacteria",
    phylum = NA,
    class = NA,
    order = NA,
    family = NA,
    genus = str_c("g_", word(taxon_name, 1)),
    species = case_when(
      word(taxon_name, 2) == "sp." ~ NA,
      is.na(word(taxon_name, 2)) ~ NA,
      TRUE ~ str_c("s_", word(taxon_name, 2))
    ),
    taxon = str_c(taxon_name)
  ) |>
  select(kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species, taxon, taxon_name)

We now filter the abundance data by first replacing the feature names in the abundance data with the taxonomic annotation from the taxonomy data, and then summing the counts of features with the same taxonomic annotation to get the count of the taxon.

Code 
abundance <-
  abundance |>
  filter(X1 != "-1") |>
  column_to_rownames(var = names(abundance)[1]) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  bind_cols(taxonomy |> select(taxon_name)) |>
  group_by(taxon_name) |>
  summarise(across(everything(), sum)) |>
  column_to_rownames("taxon_name") |>
  as.data.frame()

We filter the taxonomy data to keep only one row for each taxon, and to set the taxon names as row names.

Code 
taxonomy <-
  taxonomy |>
  distinct(taxon_name, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  column_to_rownames("taxon")

However, among “Diseased” samples, only 202 among the 348 diseased samples have been diagnosed with CDI. Do we keep all the “Diseased” samples for our analyses, or do we only keep the 202 samples diagnosed with CDI?.

I filter the dataset to keep only the 202 samples diagnosed with CDI, as well as the healthy samples (CTR).

# samples <- samples |> filter(subject_disease_status == "CDI" | subject_disease_status == "CTR")

We filter the abundance data to keep only the samples for which we have the corresponding filtered metadata.

Code 
# abundance <- abundance |>
#   select(any_of(rownames(samples)))

We will then rarefy the CDI dataset, so that all samples have the same sequencing depth, and filter out low-abundance taxa. We will use the rrarefy function from the vegan package to perform rarefaction.

First, we separate the dataset into two groups: “healthy” and “diseased” so that rarefaction (and prevalence filtering) is performed separately for the two groups, to avoid biasing the results by removing more samples from one group than the other.

Code 
tmp <-
  abundance |>
  rownames_to_column("taxon") |>
  pivot_longer(-taxon, names_to = "sample_id", values_to = "count") |>
  left_join(
    samples |> rownames_to_column("sample_id") |> select(sample_id, status),
    by = join_by(sample_id)
  )
Code 
tmp_healthy <- tmp |> filter(status == "Healthy")
tmp_diseased <- tmp |> filter(status == "Diseased")

We show the distribution of sequencing depth across samples, to choose a rarefaction depth.

Note

Note that a classical rarefaction threshold would be to simply take the median depth, but in this case, we choose to take the median depth divided by 2, to keep more samples in the dataset.

Code 
tmp_healthy |>
  group_by(sample_id) |>
  summarise(depth = sum(count)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = depth)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = median(depth)/2), color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Sequencing depth", y = "Number of samples", caption = "Red dashed line represent median depth divided by 2",
       subtitle = "Distribution of sequencing depth across healthy samples")
Code 
tmp_diseased |>
  group_by(sample_id) |>
  summarise(depth = sum(count)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = depth)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = median(depth)/2), color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Sequencing depth", y = "Number of samples", caption = "Red dashed line represent median depth divided by 2",
       subtitle = "Distribution of sequencing depth across diseased samples")

We will rarefy at a depth of median(depth)/2; this is done in the chucks below, where we also filters out samples with depth < median(depth)/2.

Code 
# for healthy samples

tmp_depth <- tmp_healthy |>
  group_by(sample_id) |>
  summarise(depth = sum(count), .groups = "drop")

min_depth <- median(tmp_depth$depth) / 2 |> round()

samples_to_keep <- tmp_depth |>
  filter(depth >= min_depth) |>
  pull(sample_id)

cat("Removing", sum(tmp_depth$depth < min_depth), "samples below depth", round(min_depth))
Removing 54 samples below depth 2421
Code 
tmp_rarefied_healthy <- tmp_healthy |>
    filter(sample_id %in% samples_to_keep) |>
    select(sample_id, taxon, count) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = taxon, values_from = count, values_fill = 0) |>
    column_to_rownames("sample_id") |>
    rrarefy(sample = min_depth) |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    rownames_to_column("sample_id") |>
    pivot_longer(-sample_id, names_to = "taxon", values_to = "count") |>
    group_by(sample_id) |>
    mutate(rel_ab = count / sum(count)) |>
    ungroup()
Code 
# for diseased samples

tmp_depth <- tmp_diseased |>
  group_by(sample_id) |>
  summarise(depth = sum(count), .groups = "drop")

min_depth <- median(tmp_depth$depth) / 2 |> round()

samples_to_keep <- tmp_depth |>
  filter(depth >= min_depth) |>
  pull(sample_id)

cat("Removing", sum(tmp_depth$depth < min_depth), "samples below depth", round(min_depth))
Removing 114 samples below depth 1085
Code 
tmp_rarefied_diseased <- tmp_diseased |>
    filter(sample_id %in% samples_to_keep) |>
    select(sample_id, taxon, count) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = taxon, values_from = count, values_fill = 0) |>
    column_to_rownames("sample_id") |>
    rrarefy(sample = min_depth) |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    rownames_to_column("sample_id") |>
    pivot_longer(-sample_id, names_to = "taxon", values_to = "count") |>
    group_by(sample_id) |>
    mutate(rel_ab = count / sum(count)) |>
    ungroup()

We convert the rarefied data back to wide format, and we merge the healthy and diseased datasets back together. Additionally, we filter the abundance data to only keep taxa for which the total count across samples is greater than 0, to remove taxa that are not present in any sample after rarefaction.

Code 
abundance <- bind_rows(tmp_rarefied_healthy, tmp_rarefied_diseased) |>
  select(sample_id, taxon, count) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = taxon, values_from = count, values_fill = 0) |>
  column_to_rownames("sample_id") |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  select(where(~ sum(.) > 0))

We finally create the phyloseq object using the otu_table, tax_table, and sample_data functions from the phyloseq package.

  tax_table(as.matrix(taxonomy)),

Healthy cohorts

In this section, we will first import the relevant datasets from the healthy cohorts, and then perform several descriptive analyses for each of those datasets. The analyses will include: The analyses will include: data cleaning, taxonomic aggregation (if necessary) and rarefaction.

Human Microbiome Project (HMP) datasets

Two datasets pertaining to the HMP will be directly imported as phyloseq objects, available directly via an R package published on GitHub, originally published in (cite). Both datasets pertains to 16S rRNA gene sequencing data and will be imported using the data function from the MicrobeDS package. The first dataset, HMPv13, contains data sequenced using the V1-V3 regions, while the second dataset, HMPv35, was sequenced using V3-V5 regions, both of them containing two time points by participant.

We import those datasets in the chunks below.

Code 
data("HMPv13")
HMPv13 <- get("HMPv13")

data("HMPv35")
HMPv35 <- get("HMPv35")

HMPv13 dataset

We visualize the structure of the HMPv13 using the phyloseq function sample_data and otu_table in the chunks below.

Code 
otu <- otu_table(HMPv13) |> as.data.frame()
sample_data <- sample_data(HMPv13) |> as_tibble()
tax_table <- tax_table(HMPv13) |> as.data.frame()

We first create a new column in the taxonomy dataset to represent the latest available taxonomic rank for each ASV, which will be used in the abundance matrix to aggregate the ASVs at the latest available taxonomic rank.

Code 
taxonomy <- 
  tax_table |> 
  rownames_to_column(var = "ASV") |> 
  mutate(
    taxon = case_when(
      !is.na(Species) ~ str_c(Genus, "_", Species),
      !is.na(Genus) ~ str_c("g_", Genus),
      !is.na(Family) ~ str_c("f_", Family),
      !is.na(Order) ~ str_c("o_", Order),
      !is.na(Class) ~ str_c("c_", Class),
      !is.na(Phylum) ~ str_c("p_", Phylum),
      TRUE ~ "Unclassified"),
    taxon_names = case_when(
      !is.na(Species) ~ str_c(Genus, " ", Species),
      !is.na(Genus) ~ str_c(Genus, " (g)"),
      !is.na(Family) ~ str_c(Family, " (f)"),
      !is.na(Order) ~ str_c(Order, " (o)"),
      !is.na(Class) ~ str_c(Class, " (c)"),
      !is.na(Phylum) ~ str_c(Phylum, " (p)"),
      TRUE ~ "Unclassified")
  )

We then aggregate the abundance matrix at the latest available taxonomic rank.

Code 
abundance <- 
  otu |> 
  rownames_to_column(var = "ASV") |> 
  left_join(taxonomy |> select(ASV, taxon), by = "ASV") |> 
  group_by(taxon) |> 
  summarise(across(-ASV, sum)) |> 
  column_to_rownames(var = "taxon")

The taxonomy dataset is also aggregated to only contain one row per unique (latest available level) taxon.

Code 
taxonomy <-
  taxonomy |>
  select(-ASV) |>
  group_by(taxon) |>
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ dplyr::first(na.omit(.x)))) |>
  ungroup() |>
  column_to_rownames(var = "taxon") |>
  clean_names()

The dataset pertains not only to stool microbiota data, but also to other microbiomes (oral, vaginal, etc.), but we will only focus on the stool microbiota data for the analyses. Therefore, we subset the abundance and sample metadata to only contain the samples pertaining to the stool microbiota. Also, we create a new column in the sample metadata to create a new sample ID that is more concise and easier to work with, while keeping the original sample names as well.

Code 
samples <-
  sample_data |>
  filter(env == "Stool") |>
  clean_names() |>
  dplyr::rename(original_id = x_sample_id) |>
  select(original_id, env) |>
  arrange(original_id) |>
  mutate(
    sample_id = str_c("HMPv13_", str_pad(row_number(), width = 3, pad = "0")),
    subject_id = str_c("S", str_pad(ceiling(row_number() / 2), width = 3, pad = "0")),
    time = case_when(row_number() %% 2 == 1 ~ 1, TRUE ~ 2),
    sample_names = sample_id
  ) |>
  column_to_rownames(var = "sample_names")

We will then rarefy the HMPv13 dataset, so that all samples have the same sequencing depth, and filter out low-abundance taxa. We will use the rrarefy function from the vegan package to perform rarefaction.

First, we separate the dataset into two groups: “healthy” and “diseased” so that rarefaction (and prevalence filtering) is performed separately for the two groups, to avoid biasing the results by removing more samples from one group than the other.

Code 
tmp <-
  abundance |>
  rownames_to_column("taxon") |>
  pivot_longer(-taxon, names_to = "sample_id", values_to = "count")

We show the distribution of sequencing depth across samples, to choose a rarefaction depth.

Note

Note that a classical rarefaction threshold would be to simply take the median depth, but in this case, we choose to take the median depth divided by 2, to keep more samples in the dataset.

Code 
tmp |>
  group_by(sample_id) |>
  summarise(depth = sum(count)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = depth)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = median(depth)/2), color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Sequencing depth", y = "Number of samples", caption = "Red dashed line represent median depth divided by 2",
       subtitle = "Distribution of sequencing depth across healthy samples")

We will rarefy at a depth of median(depth)/2; this is done in the chucks below, where we also filters out samples with depth < median(depth)/2.

Code 
tmp_depth <- tmp |>
  group_by(sample_id) |>
  summarise(depth = sum(count), .groups = "drop")

min_depth <- median(tmp_depth$depth) / 2

samples_to_keep <- tmp_depth |>
  filter(depth >= min_depth) |>
  pull(sample_id)

cat("Removing", sum(tmp_depth$depth < min_depth), "samples below depth", round(min_depth))
Removing 39 samples below depth 1941

tmp_rarefied <- tmp |>
    filter(sample_id %in% samples_to_keep) |>
    select(sample_id, taxon, count) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = taxon, values_from = count) |>
    column_to_rownames("sample_id") |>
    rrarefy(sample = min_depth) |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    rownames_to_column("sample_id") |>
    pivot_longer(-sample_id, names_to = "taxon", values_to = "count") |>
    group_by(sample_id) |>
    mutate(rel_ab = count / sum(count)) |>
    ungroup()

We convert the rarefied data back to wide format, and we merge the healthy and diseased datasets back together.

Code 
abundance <- tmp_rarefied |>
  select(sample_id, taxon, count) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = taxon, values_from = count, values_fill = 0) |>
  column_to_rownames("sample_id")

NIBIOHN and MORINAGA cohors datasets

The NIBIOHN and MORINAGA cohorts datasets were obtained from the original paper from (). The datasets were sequenced using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, but only raw reads are explicitly available. Nonetheless, I found that the authors shared a xxx as Supplementary Material, which can alternatively be used for the analyses.

Therefore, we have the following datasets at our disposal:

  • 12866_2021_2215_MOESM7_ESM.xlsx: This dataset contains the gut microbiota composition data for the NIBIOHN and MORINAGA cohorts, which can be used for the analyses. The dataset is in Excel format and contains two sheets, one for each cohort, with the abundance data for each ASV in each sample.

We import those datasets in the chunks below.

Code 
data_NIBIOHN <- read_xlsx(file.path(data_dir(), "01-raw-data/05-NIBIOHN-MORINAGA", "12866_2021_2215_MOESM7_ESM.xlsx"), skip = 2, sheet = 1)
data_MORINAGA <- read_xlsx(file.path(data_dir(), "01-raw-data/05-NIBIOHN-MORINAGA", "12866_2021_2215_MOESM7_ESM.xlsx"), skip = 2, sheet = 2)

A first look at the dataset shows that the relative abundances are scaled from 0 to 100 instead of from 0 to 1, which is the standard for relative abundance data. We will check this below, and if this is the case, we will scale the abundances back to the 0-1 range by dividing the abundance values by 100.

Code 
data_NIBIOHN |> column_to_rownames(var = names(data_NIBIOHN)[1]) |> rowSums()

Since the abundances are indeed scaled from 0 to 100, we will scale them back to the 0-1 range by dividing the abundance values by 100. We will also renormalize the abundances so that they sum to 1 for each sample, to ensure that the data is in the correct format for downstream analyses.

Code 
renorm <- function(df) {
  df |>
    column_to_rownames(var = names(df)[1]) |>
    decostand(method = "total") |>
    rownames_to_column(var = names(df)[1])
}
Code 
data_NIBIOHN <- renorm(data_NIBIOHN)
data_MORINAGA <- renorm(data_MORINAGA)

NIBIOHN cohort dataset

We first create a taxonomy dataset for the NIBIOHN cohort dataset, which will be used to aggregate the abundance matrix at the latest available taxonomic rank.

Code 
taxonomy <- 
  tibble(full_names = names(data_NIBIOHN)[-1]) |>
  mutate(
    kingdom = "k_Bacteria",
    phylum  = str_extract(full_names, "(?<=D\\.1\\.\\.)[^_]+"),
    class   = str_extract(full_names, "(?<=D\\.2\\.\\.)[^_]+"),
    order   = str_extract(full_names, "(?<=D\\.3\\.\\.)[^_]+"),
    family  = str_extract(full_names, "(?<=D\\.4\\.\\.)[^_]+"),
    genus   = str_extract(full_names, "(?<=D\\.5\\.\\.)[^_]+"),
    species = str_extract(full_names, "(?<=D\\.6\\.\\.)[^_]+")
  ) |>
  mutate(
    taxon_names =
      case_when(
        !is.na(species) ~ str_c(genus, " ", species),
        !is.na(genus) ~ str_c(genus, " (g)"),
        !is.na(family) ~ str_c(family, " (f)"),
        !is.na(order) ~ str_c(order, " (o)"),
        !is.na(class) ~ str_c(class, " (c)"),
        !is.na(phylum) ~ str_c(phylum, " (p)"),
        TRUE ~ "Unclassified"),
    taxon = case_when(
      !is.na(species) ~ str_c(genus, "_", species),
      !is.na(genus) ~ str_c("g_", genus),
      !is.na(family) ~ str_c("f_", family),
      !is.na(order) ~ str_c("o_", order),
      !is.na(class) ~ str_c("c_", class),
      !is.na(phylum) ~ str_c("p_", phylum),
      TRUE ~ "Unclassified")
  )

We check if there are any duplicated taxa in the taxonomy dataset, which will affect the aggregation of the abundance matrix.

Code 
taxonomy |> dplyr::count(taxon) |> filter(n > 1) |> gt(caption = "Duplicated taxa in the taxonomy dataset")
Duplicated taxa in the taxonomy dataset
taxon n
g_uncultured 19
g_uncultured.bacterium 14
g_uncultured.rumen.bacterium 2
Note

The duplicates in the taxonomy dataset are exclusively uncultured bacteria at the genus level, for visualization purposes, these will be aggregated, but we will keep them separated for now.

We then aggregate the abundance matrix at the latest available taxonomic rank.

Code 
abundance <- 
  data_NIBIOHN |>
  column_to_rownames(var = names(data_NIBIOHN)[1]) |>
  t() |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column(var = "full_names") |>
  left_join(taxonomy |> select(full_names, taxon), by = "full_names") |>
  group_by(taxon) |>
  summarise(across(-full_names, sum)) |>
  column_to_rownames(var = "taxon")

We also aggregate the taxonomy dataset to only contain one row per unique (latest available level) taxon. Note: All samples belong the the genus level.

Code 
taxonomy <- 
  taxonomy |>
  group_by(taxon) |>
  summarise(
    across(everything(), ~ dplyr::first(na.omit(.x)))
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  column_to_rownames(var = "taxon") |>
  select(-full_names)
Warning

Since no metadata is available for the NIBIOHN cohort dataset, we create a sample dataset with sample ID, and the samples’ type (stool samples in this case).

Code 
samples <- 
  tibble(
    sample_id = colnames(abundance),
    sample_type = "stool"
  ) |>
  column_to_rownames(var = "sample_id")

Finally, we create a new phyloseq object using the subsetted abundance matrix, taxonomy dataset, and sample metadata.

Code 
ps_NIBIOHN <- phyloseq(
  otu_table(as.matrix(abundance), taxa_are_rows = TRUE),
  tax_table(as.matrix(taxonomy)),
  sample_data(samples)
)

ps_NIBIOHN
phyloseq-class experiment-level object
otu_table()   OTU Table:         [ 351 taxa and 954 samples ]
sample_data() Sample Data:       [ 954 samples by 1 sample variables ]
tax_table()   Taxonomy Table:    [ 351 taxa by 8 taxonomic ranks ]

Dietary intervention cohort datasets

The datasets involving the dietary interventions were obtained from the original paper from (). The datasets were sequenced using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, but only raw sequences are explicitly available. Nonetheless, I found that the authors shared a gut microbiota composition dataset as Supplementary Material, which can alternatively be used for the analyses.

The study protocol involved fecal samples collected at different times, with control samples (C) and test samples (T). Specifically, fecal samples were collected at baseline (T1 and C1), after 2 weeks (T2 and C2), and after 4 weeks (T3 and C3) of the dietary intervention periods.

For the analyses, we have the following dataset at our disposal:

  • nutrients-1853911-supplementary_tables.xlsx: This dataset contains stool microbiota composition data for this cohort. The dataset is in Excel format and contains several sheets, with the abundance data for each ASV in each sample.
Code 
data <- read_xlsx(file.path(data_dir(), "01-raw-data/06-DIET", "nutrients-1853911-supplementary_tables.xlsx"), sheet = 6)

Since no metadata is available for this cohort dataset, we create a sample dataset with sample ID, the samples’ type (stool samples in this case), and the group and time point information for each sample (C1, C2, C3, T1, T2, T3).

Code 
samples <- 
  tibble(
    sample_id = names(data)[-1],
    sample_type = "stool",
    group = ifelse(str_detect(sample_id, "C"), "control", "test"),
    subgroup = case_when(
      str_detect(sample_id, "C1|T1") ~ "baseline",
      str_detect(sample_id, "C2|T2") ~ "2_weeks",
      str_detect(sample_id, "C3|T3") ~ "4_weeks",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    time = case_when(
      str_detect(sample_id, "C1|T1") ~ 1,
      str_detect(sample_id, "C2|T2") ~ 2,
      str_detect(sample_id, "C3|T3") ~ 3,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    )
  ) |>
  column_to_rownames(var = "sample_id")

The abundance matrix is created by setting the first column as row names.

Code 
abundance <- data |> column_to_rownames(var = names(data)[1]) |> t() |> as.data.frame()

We check if the samples (rows) sum to 1, which is the standard for relative abundance data. If not, we will scale the abundances so that they sum to 1 for each sample.

Code

Since the samples sum to 1, we can proceed by creating the taxonomy annotation dataframe. After manually looking at the taxonomy annotation, we see that all taxa are annotated at the genus level.

Code 
taxonomy <-
  tibble(
    full_names = colnames(abundance),
    kingdom = "k_Bacteria",
    phylum = NA,
    class = NA,
    order = NA,
    family = NA,
    genus = full_names,
    species = NA,
    taxon_names = str_c(full_names, " (g)"),
    taxon = str_c("g_", full_names)
  ) |>
  column_to_rownames(var = "full_names")

Finally, we create a new phyloseq object using the subsetted abundance matrix, taxonomy dataset, and sample metadata.

Code 
ps_DIET <- phyloseq(
  otu_table(as.matrix(abundance), taxa_are_rows = FALSE),
  tax_table(as.matrix(taxonomy)),
  sample_data(samples)
)

Supplementary cohorts

MAE integration

In this section, we will integrate the different cohorts datasets using the MultiAssayExperiment (MAE) class from Bioconductor. This class provides a convenient way to manage and analyze the cohorts.

We first transform the datasets into SummarizedExperiment objects.

Code 
# Diseased cohorts

se_ibd <- phyloseq_to_SE(ps_ibd)
se_ibs <- phyloseq_to_SE(ps_ibs)
se_cdi <- phyloseq_to_SE(ps_cdi)
se_crc <- phyloseq_to_SE(ps_crc)

# Healthy cohorts

se_hmpv13 <- phyloseq_to_SE(ps_hmpv13)
se_hmpv35 <- phyloseq_to_SE(ps_hmpv35)
se_NIBIOHN <- phyloseq_to_SE(ps_NIBIOHN)
se_MORINAGA <- phyloseq_to_SE(ps_MORINAGA)
se_DIET <- phyloseq_to_SE(ps_DIET)

We create below a MultiAssayExperiment object that contains all the SummarizedExperiment objects.

Code 
# Create a list of the SummarizedExperiment objects

se_list <- list(
  IBD = se_ibd,
  IBS = se_ibs,
  CDI = se_cdi,
  CRC = se_crc,
  HMPV13 = se_hmpv13,
  HMPV35 = se_hmpv35,
  NIBIOHN = se_NIBIOHN,
  MORINAGA = se_MORINAGA,
  DIET = se_DIET
  
)
Code 
# Create the MultiAssayExperiment object

mae <- MultiAssayExperiment(experiments = se_list)

mae
A MultiAssayExperiment object of 9 listed
 experiments with user-defined names and respective classes.
 Containing an ExperimentList class object of length 9:
 [1] IBD: SummarizedExperiment with 432 rows and 1630 columns
 [2] IBS: SummarizedExperiment with 598 rows and 62 columns
 [3] CDI: SummarizedExperiment with 868 rows and 366 columns
 [4] CRC: SummarizedExperiment with 837 rows and 575 columns
 [5] HMPV13: SummarizedExperiment with 660 rows and 171 columns
 [6] HMPV35: SummarizedExperiment with 1179 rows and 308 columns
 [7] NIBIOHN: SummarizedExperiment with 351 rows and 954 columns
 [8] MORINAGA: SummarizedExperiment with 281 rows and 642 columns
 [9] DIET: SummarizedExperiment with 193 rows and 114 columns
Functionality:
 experiments() - obtain the ExperimentList instance
 colData() - the primary/phenotype DataFrame
 sampleMap() - the sample coordination DataFrame
 `$`, `[`, `[[` - extract colData columns, subset, or experiment
 *Format() - convert into a long or wide DataFrame
 assays() - convert ExperimentList to a SimpleList of matrices
 exportClass() - save data to flat files

Saving the preprocessed MAE

We save the preprocessed MAE object as an RDS file for later use in the downstream analyses.

Code 
saveRDS(mae, file.path(data_dir(), "02-processed-data", str_c("MAE_processed_", today() |> str_remove_all("-"), ".rds")))
